screens.title: Diagnosing Layer 2 and Infrastructure Service Problems
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on the foundational services and Layer 2 features that often cause the most frustrating outages. You will learn how to spot trunk and VLAN mismatches, interpret spanning tree roles and root selection, and validate EtherChannel configuration so links form reliably. Then we shift to infrastructure services: diagnose why DHCP clients don’t receive addresses, how to confirm DNS resolution and NTP synchronization, and how to verify RADIUS or TACACS+ servers for authentication. Each idea is paired with specific show and debug commands and a concrete lab scenario that walks you through a missing ip helper-address. This matters because routing and higher-layer protocols depend on a healthy Layer 2 and consistent service availability. I’ll point out common misconceptions — for example, that a trunk showing up means all VLANs are allowed, or that PortFast is safe on any port — and show the quick commands that reveal the real state. By the end you’ll be faster at isolating where frames stop and why clients fail to get services.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Diagnosing Layer 2
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Diagnosing Layer 2 and Infrastructure Service Problems

Practical checks and commands to resolve VLAN/trunk errors, spanning-tree surprises, EtherChannel mismatches, and core service failures like DHCP, DNS, NTP, and AAA.

Layer 2 Health Map
Trunks · STP · EtherChannel
Trunk: Verify encapsulation, allowed VLANs, native VLAN
STP: Identify root and blocking ports
EtherChannel: Ensure consistent member config

In this lesson

A compact guide to find where frames or service requests stop. Each topic gives the right show/debug command and a short troubleshooting checklist you can use in the lab.

VLAN & Trunk
Check encapsulation, native VLAN, and allowed VLANs with show interfaces trunk.
DHCP
Verify helper address, pool size, and server reachability.
STP & EtherChannel
Confirm root bridge, port roles, and bundle modes for LACP/PAgP.
Quick Commands
show interfaces trunk
show spanning-tree active
show etherchannel summary
show ip dhcp binding
show ip dhcp pool
show ntp status
Explore Key Topics
VLAN Trunking
How multiple VLANs share a single link using 802.1Q and the risks of native VLAN mismatch.
DHCP Helpers
Forward DHCP broadcasts across subnets so clients receive addresses from a central server.
STP & EtherChannel
Prevent loops and aggregate links, but misconfigurations can create outages.

screens.title: Why Layer 2 and infrastructure services matter
screens.narratorSegment: Layer 2 and infrastructure services form the network's foundation. When VLANs, trunks, or STP misbehave, higher-layer routing and application services can appear broken even though the issue is local. For example, if two switches have mismatched native VLANs, untagged traffic can leak and clients can reach unexpected segments; similarly, if the intended STP root is replaced unexpectedly, traffic may take longer, congested paths. Infrastructure services — DHCP, DNS, NTP, AAA — sit logically above Layer 2 but rely on correct switching and routing to reach clients. A DHCP server in another subnet requires a helper address so broadcast requests are forwarded. A DNS server must be reachable and have the right records. NTP requires reachable associations for accurate logs. A common misconception is to treat these problems separately; in practice you must test both frame forwarding and service reachability. Start troubleshooting with simple reachability: ping the server, verify the interface and VLAN membership, and confirm the protocol-level state with show and debug commands. In short, always validate the path and the service, not just the device configuration. How will you prove the service is reachable from both client and server sides in your lab?

keyIdea.title: Check path then service
keyIdea.text: Always confirm reachability and VLAN membership before changing service configuration; many faults are path problems.

content.html:
Core Concept

Why Layer 2 and infrastructure services matter

Layer 2 problems can stop or misroute frames. Services depend on that forwarding to reach clients. Verify both layers.

Check physical and VLAN membership first: show vlan brief; show interfaces switchport.
Confirm service reachability: ping the DHCP/DNS/NTP server from the router or switch management plane.
Use protocol state commands: show spanning-tree active, show etherchannel summary, show ip dhcp binding.
Key Takeaway

Treat reachability and protocol state as equal steps: path first, then service details.

Concrete Example
A client on VLAN 20 cannot reach the DHCP server at 192.168.1.50. Verify the access port is in VLAN 20 and the router subinterface for VLAN 20 is up. If so, check for missing ip helper-address on the router subinterface. Fixing the helper address restores DHCP Offer/ACK exchange.
Common Mistake
Assuming a trunk is sufficient to carry all VLANs. A trunk may be operational but may not be allowing the needed VLANs or may have a native VLAN mismatch.
Check Your Understanding
Name two quick commands you would run first to verify a client's VLAN membership and DHCP server reachability.

screens.title: VLAN Trunking and native VLAN mismatches
screens.narratorSegment: VLAN trunking carries multiple VLANs across a single physical link using 802.1Q encapsulation. A trunk must agree on encapsulation type and which VLANs are allowed. A frequent troublemaker is a native VLAN mismatch: one side treats VLAN X as untagged while the other tags it or expects a different native VLAN. That mismatch can cause untagged frames to be accepted on the wrong VLAN or BPDUs to be dropped, leading to STP instability. To diagnose trunks start with show interfaces trunk to confirm trunking state, encapsulation, and native VLAN. Then use show interfaces switchport for the physical details and switchport trunk allowed vlan to confirm permitted VLANs. Example: if a user in VLAN 20 cannot reach servers in VLAN 20, verify that VLAN 20 is allowed and active across all trunks between the user’s access switch and the server’s switch. A common misconception is to assume that seeing the physical link up means the trunk is correct; always verify allowed VLANs and native VLAN explicitly. Key takeaway: validate encapsulation, native VLAN, and allowed list before changing downstream device settings. VLAN Trunking and native VLAN mismatches means a trunk can be up but still misconfigured for encapsulation, native vlan, or allowed vlans—check all three.. In practical terms, detecting mismatched encapsulation, allowed vlans, and native vlans. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

VLAN Trunking and native VLAN mismatches

Trunks carry multiple VLANs with tagging. A native VLAN mismatch causes untagged frames to be misclassified and can destabilize STP.

show interfaces trunk → trunk status, encapsulation, native
show interfaces switchport → port mode and access/trunk details
show vlan brief → confirm VLAN presence and active ports
Diagnostic Flow
  1. Confirm trunk operational: show interfaces trunk.
  2. Check encapsulation matches on both ends (dot1q).
  3. Verify native VLAN on both sides is identical.
  4. Ensure required VLANs are allowed: switchport trunk allowed vlan.
Concrete Scenario
User in VLAN 20 cannot reach servers on VLAN 20. You run show interfaces trunk and find VLAN 20 is not allowed across the aggregation. Adding VLAN 20 to the allowed list restores connectivity.
Key Takeaway

Trunk links must match encapsulation, native VLAN, and allowed VLANs — one mismatch can break connectivity.

screens.title: Spanning Tree Protocol troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Spanning Tree Protocol prevents loops by creating a loop-free tree of the switched network. The switch with the lowest Bridge ID becomes the root; Bridge ID combines priority and MAC, so an unexpected root usually means a device with an unintended low priority or default priority was introduced. Use show spanning-tree active to identify the root and check port roles such as Root, Designated, Alternate, or Blocked. If a port is blocking unexpectedly, inspect its port cost and path to the root; misapplied root guard, BPDU guard, or incorrect priorities can change roles. PortFast is helpful on edge ports to immediately forward host traffic, but enabling PortFast on trunk ports is dangerous because it bypasses STP convergence and can create temporary loops. If BPDU Guard automatically shuts down a port, it means a BPDU arrived on a PortFast-enabled interface — often a sign of an unauthorized switch. A common misconception is that enabling features like PortFast universally increases stability; in reality, PortFast should only be used on true edge access ports. Close your troubleshooting by determining the correct root bridge candidate and adjusting priorities or using root primary commands to reestablish the intended topology.

keyIdea.text: Find the root and verify port roles; PortFast and BPDU Guard must be applied only at appropriate edges.

content.html:
Core Concept

Spanning Tree Protocol troubleshooting

Use show spanning-tree active to find the root bridge and port roles. Mis-elections cause suboptimal forwarding or downtime.

show spanning-tree active → root and per-VLAN port roles
Check Bridge ID: priority and MAC determine the root
If root is wrong, set explicit priority or run root primary on intended switch
Misconfiguration Example
A newly-installed access switch used default priority and became the root. Traffic took nonoptimal paths causing congestion. The fix was to configure the intended core switch with a lower priority and set the access switch to a higher priority.
PortFast and BPDU Guard
PortFast immediately forwards host ports but should not be enabled on ports connecting to other switches. BPDU Guard disables a port on BPDU receipt, protecting topology but requiring investigation when triggered.
Key Takeaway

Confirm the root and port roles and apply PortFast/BPDU Guard only on true edge ports to avoid topology disruption.

screens.title: EtherChannel: common faults and checks
screens.narratorSegment: EtherChannel aggregates multiple physical interfaces into one logical link to increase bandwidth and provide redundancy. Troubleshooting typically centers on three root causes. First, mode mismatch: protocols like LACP and PAgP require compatible modes — for LACP the usual working pair is active-active or passive-active; configuring one side as active and the other as on or a mismatched protocol will prevent formation. Second, configuration inconsistency: member interfaces must match in speed, duplex, allowed VLANs, and native VLAN; any difference can keep a member out of the bundle. Third, port-channel state: even when members look correct, the logical port-channel interface can be down. Use show etherchannel summary to see bundle status and member roles and show interfaces port-channel for the logical interface details. A common misconception is that simply configuring channel-group on two switches guarantees aggregation — you must ensure both sides agree on protocol and per-interface settings. Example: if load balancing does not distribute traffic evenly, confirm the hashing algorithm and member states. Close troubleshooting by correcting mismatched modes or aligning member configs and then verifying traffic flows across the channel.

keyIdea.title: Consistency required
keyIdea.text: All member ports must match in mode and settings; mode mismatches are the most common failure point.

content.html:
Comparison

EtherChannel faults: Mode vs Configuration

Mode Mismatch: LACP vs PAgP vs static. Use show etherchannel summary to identify negotiation failures.
Config Inconsistency: speed/duplex, native VLAN, allowed VLANs must match on every member interface.
Port-channel State: check the logical interface with show interfaces port-channel <n> to confirm up/up.
Diagnostic Commands
show etherchannel summary → bundle and member status. show interfaces port-channel <n> → logical interface details. show running-config interface <int> → verify per-interface settings.
Concrete Example
One side was set to LACP active and the other to channel-group mode on (no LACP). The bundle did not form. Changing both sides to LACP active fixed the aggregation.
Key Takeaway

Ensure matching protocols and identical interface settings. Use show etherchannel summary to uncover mode mismatch quickly.

screens.title: Troubleshooting DHCP failures and helper-addresses
screens.narratorSegment: DHCP provides automatic IP configuration but depends on correct forwarding when the server is in another subnet. Start by verifying that the client’s access port is in the intended VLAN and that the VLAN exists on all intermediate switches. Use show vlan brief and show interfaces switchport. If the client’s VLAN and switchport are correct, check the router subinterface for the VLAN. If the DHCP server is remote, there must be an ip helper-address configured on the router interface for that VLAN so broadcasts are forwarded to the server. A concrete configuration example: the client on VLAN 20 uses 10.0.20.10; the router subinterface GigabitEthernet0/0.20 needs encapsulation dot1Q 20, ip address 10.0.20.1, and ip helper-address 192.168.1.50. You can confirm assignment on the server side with show ip dhcp binding and on the router with show ip interface to see the helper configured. If offers don't reach the client, use debug ip dhcp server packet on the DHCP server to see Discover/Offer exchanges. A common misconception is to try changing pool settings before verifying helper-address and reachability. Always prove the broadcast path exists before modifying DHCP scopes or options. After adding the helper address, a client retry should produce an IP via DHCP Offer and ACK.

keyIdea.title: Forward broadcasts
keyIdea.text: If DHCP server is remote, ip helper-address on the gateway is required to forward client broadcasts to the server.

content.html:
Process Flow

Troubleshooting DHCP failures and helper-addresses

Verify VLAN membership, router subinterface, and helper address before changing server scopes.

Show Commands
  • show vlan brief
  • show interfaces switchport
  • show ip interface
  • show ip dhcp binding
Key Takeaway

Always confirm the helper address and path to the DHCP server before altering pools.

Configuration Example
! Switch A (access port)
SwitchA(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
SwitchA(config-if)# switchport mode access
SwitchA(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SwitchA(config-if)# no shutdown

! Router R1 subinterface (problematic initially)
RouterR1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
RouterR1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 20
RouterR1(config-subif)# ip address 10.0.20.1 255.255.255.0
RouterR1(config-subif)# no shutdown

! Fix: add helper address
RouterR1(config-subif)# ip helper-address 192.168.1.50
After configuring the helper address, verify with show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20 and then test the client obtaining an IP. On the DHCP server use show ip dhcp binding to confirm assignment or debug ip dhcp server packet to watch the transaction.

screens.title: DHCP scope exhaustion and server-side checks
screens.narratorSegment: DHCP scope exhaustion happens when all addresses in a pool are assigned and new clients cannot obtain an IP. To diagnose this, inspect the DHCP server pool status with show ip dhcp pool which reports statistics and how many addresses remain. On the server examine show ip dhcp binding to list active leases and their associated MAC addresses. If no addresses are available, the remedy may be expanding the pool, reclaiming stale leases, or creating additional scopes. Another common issue is incorrect scope options — wrong default gateway or DNS addresses — which do not stop lease assignment but break client connectivity to essential services; verify scopes are configured with the correct options. When a client fails to receive a lease yet the pool shows available addresses, verify network reachability and helper addresses back at the router. Use debug ip dhcp server packet on the server while a client attempts a lease to view Discover and Offer flows. A misconception is to assume pool exhaustion is rare; in dynamic environments with many short leases it can happen quickly. Finally, log your change and test with a client to ensure leases are assigned and options propagate correctly.

keyIdea.text: Use show ip dhcp pool and show ip dhcp binding to determine whether the server has addresses and whether leases exist for clients.

content.html:
Definition

DHCP pool exhaustion and server-side checks

Confirm pool capacity then verify bindings and options before changing network devices.

show ip dhcp pool → remaining addresses and pool statistics
show ip dhcp binding → current leases and MAC associations
debug ip dhcp server packet → observe Discover/Offer/Request/ACK exchanges
Concrete Example
An office with many transient devices had 100 addresses allocated and 120 devices; new devices failed to get leases. The solution was to resize the pool and reduce unnecessary short-term leases, and to add monitoring to alert when pool usage exceeds 85%.
Common Mistake
Changing network switch settings before confirming the server still has available addresses. Always check the server pool first.
Key Takeaway

Pool limits and incorrect scope options are frequent causes of DHCP service failures; verify bindings and options before changing network behavior.

screens.title: DNS and NTP troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: DNS translates hostnames to IP addresses and failures typically present as the ability to reach an IP but not a hostname. Start by checking which DNS servers clients have — often via DHCP options — and confirm those servers are reachable using ping. On routers use show ip name-servers to see configured servers and then attempt resolution using a simple ping by name from the router after configuring ip name-server. Tools like nslookup or dig from a client or server help identify whether the server has the record. If servers are unreachable check routing and firewall rules. NTP synchronizes clocks; inaccurate device clocks degrade logs and certificate validation. Use show ntp status and show ntp associations to see synchronization state. If an NTP server is unreachable check network reachability and ensure authentication keys match if authentication is used. A common misconception is to assume NTP is a convenience; in distributed systems and security audits, accurate timestamps are essential. Example: if a device shows stratum 16 or no association, identify whether the server IP is correct and reachable, then correct the ntp server configuration. Both DNS and NTP troubleshooting follow the same pattern: verify configured servers, test reachability, and confirm the service returns expected answers.

keyIdea.title: Name and time must work
keyIdea.text: Confirm DNS servers and NTP associations are reachable and returning valid replies before investigating applications.

Definition

DNS and NTP troubleshooting

Check configured name servers and NTP servers, verify reachability, and test responses to prove service health.

DNS: verify client DNS via DHCP, ping DNS server, use nslookup to test resolution.
NTP: show ntp status and show ntp associations to confirm synchronization.
Concrete Example
Users can ping 8.8.8.8 but cannot browse by name. On the gateway, show ip name-servers reveals an incorrect server IP. After correcting ip name-server and confirming ping succeeds, hostnames resolve and browsing works again.
Check Your Understanding
When NTP shows no association, what two quick checks should you perform before changing server configuration? (Answer: ping for reachability and verify authentication keys if used.)
Key Takeaway

DNS and NTP troubleshooting are reachability-first tasks; confirm the server and then the protocol response.

screens.title: AAA service troubleshooting (RADIUS/TACACS+)
screens.narratorSegment: AAA services control who can log in, what they can do, and how actions are recorded. Authentication failures often stem from reachability issues or mismatched shared secrets. Start by confirming the AAA server IP is reachable with ping and that the server is listening for the expected protocol and port. On the network device, check the configured AAA servers and shared secret entries using show aaa servers or your device-specific show commands. If users authenticate but cannot run certain commands, the issue is an authorization policy mismatch; verify server-side profiles and device request attributes. Accounting failures often go unnoticed until audits require logs; ensure accounting destinations are reachable and accounting rules are applied. Use debug aaa authentication to watch the authentication exchange when a user attempts login and review server logs to correlate attempts. A common misconception is to change local authentication as a first step; instead, verify connectivity and shared secrets. When a server is unreachable, temporarily falling back to local authentication allows access while you restore AAA connectivity, but always record and later reconcile accounting gaps. Finish troubleshooting by validating reachability, testing with an explicit test user, and observing both device and server logs for the transaction details.

keyIdea.text: Start AAA troubleshooting with ping and show aaa servers; use debug traces to capture the authentication exchange.

content.html:
Process Flow

AAA service troubleshooting

Authentication, authorization, and accounting require reachable servers and matching secrets; verify both sides.

show aaa servers → server list and reachability
ping → basic reachability
debug aaa authentication → observe authentication flow
Concrete Example
Users cannot log in because the RADIUS server moved IPs. A ping from the switch failed. After updating the server entry and secret, authentication succeeded and accounting entries resumed.
Common Mistake
Changing local authentication before confirming the AAA server is reachable can hide root causes and complicate rollback.
Key Takeaway

Confirm AAA server reachability and shared secrets, then use debug traces and server logs to complete diagnosis.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: DHCP helper-address lab walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This lab walks you through a realistic DHCP failure and the steps to fix it. Start by creating the topology: Switch A with GigabitEthernet0/1 connecting the PC, Router R1 with subinterface GigabitEthernet0/0.20 for VLAN 20, and a DHCP server at 192.168.1.50. Apply the initial configurations: the switch access port in VLAN 20 and the router subinterface with correct encapsulation and IP but without an ip helper-address. Reproduce the failure: attempt to obtain an IP on the PC and observe no lease. Troubleshooting steps: first run show vlan brief and show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/1 switchport on the switch to confirm VLAN membership. On the router check show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20 to confirm the subinterface is up. If the server is remote, the fix is to configure ip helper-address 192.168.1.50 on the router subinterface. After configuring, verify with show ip dhcp binding on the server and then attempt the client lease again. If leases still fail, run debug ip dhcp server packet on the DHCP server to watch the exchange. This lab reinforces the approach: verify path, confirm service reachability, then fix the protocol forwarding configuration.

keyIdea.text: Reproduce the failure, validate VLAN and subinterface state, then add ip helper-address and confirm DHCP bindings.

content.html:
Practical Lab

DHCP helper-address lab walkthrough

Follow the steps to reproduce a missing helper address and restore DHCP service.

Step 1: Configure Switch A access port to VLAN 20. Verify with show vlan brief.
Step 2: Confirm Router subinterface has encapsulation and IP. Use show ip interface.
Step 3: Attempt DHCP lease on PC; if fail, add ip helper-address on router subinterface.
Step 4: Verify with show ip dhcp binding on server and test client lease.
Verification Commands
show vlan brief | show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/1 switchport | show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20 | show ip dhcp binding
Scenario Config (starter)
! Switch A (starter)
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 20
 no shutdown

! Router R1 (starter)
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 20
 ip address 10.0.20.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
TODO: add ip helper-address 192.168.1.50 on the router subinterface to restore DHCP for VLAN 20.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these key concepts in mind when diagnosing Layer 2 and service issues. VLAN trunking uses 802.1Q to carry multiple VLANs and requires matching encapsulation and allowed lists. A native VLAN mismatch often causes untagged frames to leak or STP instability. Spanning Tree Protocol elects a root bridge based on Bridge ID; ensure the intended root has the lowest priority to keep paths optimal. PortFast and BPDU Guard are powerful edge features but must be applied only on true access ports to avoid unintended topology changes. Use the commands shown in the lesson to prove the state before changing configuration. These concepts form the checklist you use in every troubleshooting session: verify physical and VLAN state, prove reachability to services, inspect protocol state, and then correct only what you can prove is wrong.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts

VLAN Trunking
Carry multiple VLANs over one link with 802.1Q; confirm encapsulation and allowed VLANs.
Native VLAN Mismatch
Different native VLANs between trunk ends cause untagged traffic leakage and STP issues.
STP Root Bridge
Lowest Bridge ID (priority + MAC) becomes root; ensure intended device has lowest priority.
EtherChannel
Bundle links for bandwidth and redundancy; member ports must match and modes must be compatible.
DHCP Helper Address
Forward DHCP broadcasts from a subnet to a remote server using ip helper-address on the gateway.
DNS, NTP & AAA
DNS for names, NTP for time, AAA for access — all require reachability and correct server configuration.
Summary: When troubleshooting start with reachability and VLAN/frame verification, then inspect protocol-specific state with show/debug commands before changing configuration.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Quick Reference

What to Remember

Diagnostic Commands
Use show interfaces trunk, show spanning-tree active, and show etherchannel summary to reveal root causes quickly.

Access port → trunk → gateway → server. Confirm each hop before changing configs.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on the foundational services and Layer 2 features that often cause the most frustrating outages. You will learn how to spot trunk and VLAN mismatches, interpret spanning tree roles and root selection, and validate EtherChannel configuration so links form reliably. Then we shift to infrastructure services: diagnose why DHCP clients don’t receive addresses, how to confirm DNS resolution and NTP synchronization, and how to verify RADIUS or TACACS+ servers for authentication. Each idea is paired with specific show and debug commands and a concrete lab scenario that walks you through a missing ip helper-address. This matters because routing and higher-layer protocols depend on a healthy Layer 2 and consistent service availability. I’ll point out common misconceptions — for example, that a trunk showing up means all VLANs are allowed, or that PortFast is safe on any port — and show the quick commands that reveal the real state. By the end you’ll be faster at isolating where frames stop and why clients fail to get services.

These objectives focus your practice and the lab. First, you will troubleshoot VLAN and trunking issues so that traffic flows only on the intended VLANs. That includes detecting mismatched encapsulation and native VLANs that let untagged frames leak across segments. Second, you will diagnose Spanning Tree Protocol behavior, recognize a mis-elected root bridge, and interpret port roles so you can restore optimal paths. Third, you will resolve EtherChannel connectivity and load-balancing faults by checking compatible modes, member consistency, and the port-channel state. Fourth, you will identify and fix DHCP failures by verifying reachability, helper addresses, and pool capacity. Each objective pairs a practical command set and a short checklist to make your troubleshooting systematic and repeatable in a lab or production environment. Learning Objectives means master targeted show/debug commands and simple configuration checks to resolve common layer 2 and service faults.. In practical terms, what you will be able to do after this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

These extended objectives prepare you for assessment scenarios and the hands-on lab. You will diagnose DHCP-specific failures such as helper address misconfiguration and IP pool exhaustion, and you will validate DHCP transactions using server-side bindings and debug output. You will practice DNS troubleshooting by confirming configured name servers and using resolution tests from routers or clients to prove where name resolution fails. You will also verify NTP synchronization, including association checks and reachability, because accurate time is critical for logs and security. Lastly, you will troubleshoot AAA service failures by checking reachability, shared secrets, and server-side policies so authentication and authorization work correctly. Each objective is action-oriented and tied to a command or verification step you will perform during the lab checklist. Learning Objectives — Extended Skills means pair each troubleshooting claim with a specific show or debug command to prove the root cause before you change configuration.. In practical terms, prepare lab tasks and assessment items. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Layer 2 and infrastructure services form the network's foundation. When VLANs, trunks, or STP misbehave, higher-layer routing and application services can appear broken even though the issue is local. For example, if two switches have mismatched native VLANs, untagged traffic can leak and clients can reach unexpected segments; similarly, if the intended STP root is replaced unexpectedly, traffic may take longer, congested paths. Infrastructure services — DHCP, DNS, NTP, AAA — sit logically above Layer 2 but rely on correct switching and routing to reach clients. A DHCP server in another subnet requires a helper address so broadcast requests are forwarded. A DNS server must be reachable and have the right records. NTP requires reachable associations for accurate logs. A common misconception is to treat these problems separately; in practice you must test both frame forwarding and service reachability. Start troubleshooting with simple reachability: ping the server, verify the interface and VLAN membership, and confirm the protocol-level state with show and debug commands. In short, always validate the path and the service, not just the device configuration. How will you prove the service is reachable from both client and server sides in your lab?

VLAN trunking carries multiple VLANs across a single physical link using 802.1Q encapsulation. A trunk must agree on encapsulation type and which VLANs are allowed. A frequent troublemaker is a native VLAN mismatch: one side treats VLAN X as untagged while the other tags it or expects a different native VLAN. That mismatch can cause untagged frames to be accepted on the wrong VLAN or BPDUs to be dropped, leading to STP instability. To diagnose trunks start with show interfaces trunk to confirm trunking state, encapsulation, and native VLAN. Then use show interfaces switchport for the physical details and switchport trunk allowed vlan to confirm permitted VLANs. Example: if a user in VLAN 20 cannot reach servers in VLAN 20, verify that VLAN 20 is allowed and active across all trunks between the user’s access switch and the server’s switch. A common misconception is to assume that seeing the physical link up means the trunk is correct; always verify allowed VLANs and native VLAN explicitly. Key takeaway: validate encapsulation, native VLAN, and allowed list before changing downstream device settings. VLAN Trunking and native VLAN mismatches means a trunk can be up but still misconfigured for encapsulation, native vlan, or allowed vlans—check all three.. In practical terms, detecting mismatched encapsulation, allowed vlans, and native vlans. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Spanning Tree Protocol prevents loops by creating a loop-free tree of the switched network. The switch with the lowest Bridge ID becomes the root; Bridge ID combines priority and MAC, so an unexpected root usually means a device with an unintended low priority or default priority was introduced. Use show spanning-tree active to identify the root and check port roles such as Root, Designated, Alternate, or Blocked. If a port is blocking unexpectedly, inspect its port cost and path to the root; misapplied root guard, BPDU guard, or incorrect priorities can change roles. PortFast is helpful on edge ports to immediately forward host traffic, but enabling PortFast on trunk ports is dangerous because it bypasses STP convergence and can create temporary loops. If BPDU Guard automatically shuts down a port, it means a BPDU arrived on a PortFast-enabled interface — often a sign of an unauthorized switch. A common misconception is that enabling features like PortFast universally increases stability; in reality, PortFast should only be used on true edge access ports. Close your troubleshooting by determining the correct root bridge candidate and adjusting priorities or using root primary commands to reestablish the intended topology.

EtherChannel aggregates multiple physical interfaces into one logical link to increase bandwidth and provide redundancy. Troubleshooting typically centers on three root causes. First, mode mismatch: protocols like LACP and PAgP require compatible modes — for LACP the usual working pair is active-active or passive-active; configuring one side as active and the other as on or a mismatched protocol will prevent formation. Second, configuration inconsistency: member interfaces must match in speed, duplex, allowed VLANs, and native VLAN; any difference can keep a member out of the bundle. Third, port-channel state: even when members look correct, the logical port-channel interface can be down. Use show etherchannel summary to see bundle status and member roles and show interfaces port-channel for the logical interface details. A common misconception is that simply configuring channel-group on two switches guarantees aggregation — you must ensure both sides agree on protocol and per-interface settings. Example: if load balancing does not distribute traffic evenly, confirm the hashing algorithm and member states. Close troubleshooting by correcting mismatched modes or aligning member configs and then verifying traffic flows across the channel.

DHCP provides automatic IP configuration but depends on correct forwarding when the server is in another subnet. Start by verifying that the client’s access port is in the intended VLAN and that the VLAN exists on all intermediate switches. Use show vlan brief and show interfaces switchport. If the client’s VLAN and switchport are correct, check the router subinterface for the VLAN. If the DHCP server is remote, there must be an ip helper-address configured on the router interface for that VLAN so broadcasts are forwarded to the server. A concrete configuration example: the client on VLAN 20 uses 10.0.20.10; the router subinterface GigabitEthernet0/0.20 needs encapsulation dot1Q 20, ip address 10.0.20.1, and ip helper-address 192.168.1.50. You can confirm assignment on the server side with show ip dhcp binding and on the router with show ip interface to see the helper configured. If offers don't reach the client, use debug ip dhcp server packet on the DHCP server to see Discover/Offer exchanges. A common misconception is to try changing pool settings before verifying helper-address and reachability. Always prove the broadcast path exists before modifying DHCP scopes or options. After adding the helper address, a client retry should produce an IP via DHCP Offer and ACK.

DHCP scope exhaustion happens when all addresses in a pool are assigned and new clients cannot obtain an IP. To diagnose this, inspect the DHCP server pool status with show ip dhcp pool which reports statistics and how many addresses remain. On the server examine show ip dhcp binding to list active leases and their associated MAC addresses. If no addresses are available, the remedy may be expanding the pool, reclaiming stale leases, or creating additional scopes. Another common issue is incorrect scope options — wrong default gateway or DNS addresses — which do not stop lease assignment but break client connectivity to essential services; verify scopes are configured with the correct options. When a client fails to receive a lease yet the pool shows available addresses, verify network reachability and helper addresses back at the router. Use debug ip dhcp server packet on the server while a client attempts a lease to view Discover and Offer flows. A misconception is to assume pool exhaustion is rare; in dynamic environments with many short leases it can happen quickly.
